To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

* We define a meta-reinforcement-learning problem that can be used to evaluate whether a meta-learner is actually learning to use the structure embedded within a task distribution, rather than simply learning the statistical structure of the tasks.

(1) we introduce a new meta-RL task that is generated using a structured task distribution, (2) we introduce a null task distribution that is statistically complex but lacks the explicit rule-based task structure used in the original structured task, (3) we find that humans do significantly better than meta-learners in the structured task, and significantly worse in the null task, whereas meta-learners do significantly better in the null than in the structured task.

(1) humans are better than meta-learned agents at learning structured task distributions, and (2) humans are better at learning structured task distribution than unstructured task distribution, while meta-learned reinforcement learners are not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: what is the role of structure in learning?
the question of what makes humans and machines different, and how we can use this understanding to improve machine performance.
understanding how meta-learning works, and how it differs between humans and machines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
meta-learning is not a panacea for learning structured representations in neural networks.
The results suggest that the meta-learner has learned to use the structure embedded in the tasks, but it is not using the structure in the way that human learners do.
meta-learned agents are better at learning null tasks, whereas humans are better at learning structured tasks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
meta-learners and humans can learn the same tasks, and can do so in a way that is similar, but not identical.
meta-learning is not the silver bullet that we might hope for, and that we need to better understand how meta-learning works to understand its potential.
We introduce a new meta-RL task in which a compositional task grammar is used to create a structured task distribution.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we can learn about the nature of meta-learning by constructing task distributions in which there are multiple ways of solving a problem, and then comparing how humans and machines perform across the task distributions.
the way we evaluate meta-learning is important.
meta-learning agents may be learning strategies that are different from humans.
